statement: If two straight lines incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them medial, but the rectangle contained by them rational, be added together, the whole straight line is irrational; and let it be called the side of a rational plus a medial area.
heath_proof: For let two straight lines AB, BC incommensurable in square, and fulfilling the given conditions [X. 34], be added together; I say that AC is irrational. For, since the sum of the squares on AB, BC is medial, while twice the rectangle AB, BC is rational, therefore the sum of the squares on AB, BC is incommensurable with twice the rectangle AB, BC; so that the square on AC is also incommensurable with twice the rectangle AB, BC. [X. 16] But twice the rectangle AB, BC is rational; therefore the square on AC is irrational. Therefore AC is irrational. [X. Def. 4] And let it be called the side of a rational plus a medial area.

**Statement:** If two straight lines incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them medial, but the rectangle contained by them rational, be added together, the whole straight line is irrational; and let it be called the side of a rational plus a medial area.

**Step 1.** Let AB, BC be two straight lines incommensurable in square, placed in a straight line so that AC is the whole, and let them satisfy the hypothesis: the sum of the squares on AB, BC is medial, while the rectangle AB, BC is rational. Let R denote the rational square set out (the square on the assigned rational straight line). I say that AC is irrational.

**Step 2.** Since AC is cut at B, the square on AC is equal to the squares on AB, BC together with twice the rectangle AB, BC [2.4]. Write S for the sum of the squares on AB, BC, so that the square on AC is equal to S together with twice the rectangle AB, BC.

**Step 3.** Twice the rectangle AB, BC has to the rectangle AB, BC the ratio which the number 2 has to the number 1; therefore twice the rectangle AB, BC is commensurable with the rectangle AB, BC [10.6].

**Step 4.** The rectangle AB, BC is rational, that is, it is commensurable with the rational square R [D10.1.4]. Since twice the rectangle AB, BC is commensurable with the rectangle AB, BC (Step 3), and the rectangle AB, BC is commensurable with R, twice the rectangle AB, BC is commensurable with R [10.12]; hence twice the rectangle AB, BC is rational [D10.1.4].

**Step 5.** S, the sum of the squares on AB, BC, is medial, that is, it is equal to the square on a medial straight line, which square is equal to a rectangle contained by rational straight lines commensurable in square only; such a rectangle is irrational [10.21]. Therefore S is an irrational area, that is, S is incommensurable with the rational square R [D10.1.4].

**Step 6.** Twice the rectangle AB, BC and R are commensurable (Step 4), and R is incommensurable with S (Step 5); therefore twice the rectangle AB, BC is also incommensurable with S [10.13].

**Step 7.** Thus S and twice the rectangle AB, BC are two incommensurable magnitudes, and when they are added together the whole is the square on AC (Step 2). Therefore the square on AC is incommensurable with each of them, and in particular with twice the rectangle AB, BC [10.16].

**Step 8.** Twice the rectangle AB, BC is commensurable with R (Step 4), and it is incommensurable with the square on AC (Step 7); therefore R is also incommensurable with the square on AC [10.13]. Hence the square on AC is irrational, being incommensurable with the rational square R, and therefore AC, the straight line which produces it, is irrational [D10.1.4].

**Step 9.** Therefore, if two straight lines incommensurable in square which make the sum of the squares on them medial but the rectangle contained by them rational be added together, the whole straight line is irrational; and let it be called the side of a rational plus a medial area. Q.E.D.
